items.q: Why is childhood cancer treated differently from adult cancer?
items.a: Childhood cancer is treated differently because it arises mostly from developmental abnormalities rather than accumulated lifestyle exposures, and children's cancers tend to be highly chemosensitive with distinct treatment protocols and dosing. This is why paediatric oncology is its own medical specialty rather than a scaled-down version of adult cancer care. Treatment decisions are made by specialists trained specifically in childhood cancer biology.

items.q: What are the most common cancers in children?
items.a: The most common childhood cancers are acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (about a quarter of cases), brain and central nervous system tumours, and embryonal tumours such as neuroblastoma and Wilms tumour. This distribution is very different from adult cancer, where solid tumours from organs like the lung, breast, and colon predominate. The specific subtype and molecular features determine the treatment approach.

items.q: Is childhood cancer usually curable?
items.a: Many childhood cancers have high cure rates — for example, favourable-histology Wilms tumour and standard-risk ALL both exceed 85-90% cure rates with modern protocols. Outcomes vary significantly by cancer type, subtype, stage, and response to initial treatment, so no single survival figure applies to every child. A paediatric oncology team can give a realistic outlook based on your child's specific diagnosis.

items.q: What causes cancer in children?
items.a: Most childhood cancers are not linked to lifestyle or environmental factors the way many adult cancers are — they typically arise from developmental abnormalities, such as chromosomal translocations or fusion genes that occur during rapid fetal or childhood cell growth. In most cases, no clear preventable cause is identified. Genetic counselling may be recommended in specific situations where a hereditary cancer syndrome is suspected.

items.q: How is childhood cancer diagnosed and staged?
items.a: Diagnosis typically involves imaging (such as MRI, CT, or PET scans), biopsy with detailed pathology review, and increasingly molecular or genomic testing to identify the specific subtype. Staging depends on the cancer type and may include bone marrow testing for leukaemias or lymphomas, or surgical staging for solid tumours. These results together guide risk stratification and treatment planning by the paediatric oncology team.

items.q: What advanced treatments are available for childhood cancer beyond chemotherapy?
items.a: Advanced options include CAR-T cell therapy for relapsed or refractory leukaemia and lymphoma, proton beam radiation for brain and spinal tumours, molecular targeted drugs matched to specific genetic mutations, and clinical trials of emerging therapies. The appropriate option depends on the exact cancer subtype, molecular profile, and how the child has responded to prior treatment. These are reviewed and recommended by a paediatric oncology specialist.

items.q: Is CAR-T cell therapy available for children?
items.a: Yes, tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah) is an FDA-approved CAR-T therapy for children and young adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, achieving remission in a majority of patients where standard salvage chemotherapy has much lower success. Eligibility depends on leukaemia subtype, prior treatment, and overall health, confirmed through specialist review. Additional paediatric CAR-T trials are active for other blood cancers.

items.q: Why is proton beam therapy often preferred for children over standard radiation?
items.a: Proton beam therapy deposits its radiation dose more precisely than conventional X-ray radiation, reducing exposure to surrounding healthy, still-developing tissue. This matters especially for brain, spinal, and head/neck tumours in children, where minimizing long-term cardiac, pulmonary, and neurocognitive damage is a major treatment goal. Availability and suitability depend on tumour location and treatment centre access.

items.q: Does molecular or genomic testing matter for childhood cancer treatment?
items.a: Yes, genomic profiling is now standard for many paediatric brain tumours, sarcomas, and refractory leukaemias, since specific mutations such as NTRK fusions can be matched to targeted drugs with strong response rates regardless of the tumour's location. Not every childhood cancer has an actionable mutation, so results vary by case. Testing is typically arranged through the treating paediatric oncology centre.

items.q: Are clinical trials a standard part of childhood cancer treatment?
items.a: Yes, for many childhood cancers, clinical trial participation is considered part of standard care rather than a last resort, since collaborative groups define treatment protocols through ongoing trials. This is especially true for rare paediatric cancers, where a trial may be the only source of the most current treatment approach. Enrollment always depends on eligibility criteria reviewed by the trial investigators.

items.q: What long-term effects can childhood cancer treatment cause?
items.a: Depending on the treatment received, long-term effects can include heart problems from certain chemotherapy drugs, neurocognitive changes from brain radiation or intrathecal chemotherapy, hormone deficiencies, and a small increased risk of a second cancer later in life. Not every survivor experiences these effects, and risk depends on the specific drugs, doses, and radiation received. Lifelong survivorship monitoring helps catch and manage issues early.

items.q: Why does my child need lifelong follow-up after finishing cancer treatment?
items.a: Because many childhood cancer survivors live 50 to 70 years after treatment, ongoing monitoring helps detect potential late effects on the heart, hormones, cognition, or risk of secondary cancers before they become serious. Follow-up schedules and tests depend on the specific chemotherapy and radiation your child received. A paediatric oncology survivorship programme can outline the right monitoring plan.

items.q: Will my child's cancer treatment affect their growth or development?
items.a: Some treatments, particularly cranial radiation and certain chemotherapy regimens, can affect growth hormone levels, puberty, and in some cases learning or memory, especially in children treated at a younger age. Not all children are affected, and the risk depends on the specific treatment given. Endocrine and neurocognitive monitoring during survivorship care can identify and address these issues.

items.q: Can childhood cancer come back after successful treatment?
items.a: Relapse is possible for some childhood cancers, and the risk depends on the original diagnosis, subtype, and how the cancer responded to initial treatment. This is one reason structured follow-up imaging and testing continue for years after treatment ends. Your child's oncology team can explain the specific relapse risk and monitoring plan for their type of cancer.

items.q: What support exists for siblings and parents during childhood cancer treatment?
items.a: Leading paediatric cancer centres typically offer family support services including counselling, sibling support programmes, school liaison, and psycho-oncology care, recognizing that a childhood cancer diagnosis affects the whole family. Availability varies by treatment centre and country. Asking about these services early in treatment planning can help the whole family cope through a difficult period.

items.q: How much does advanced pediatric cancer treatment cost?
items.a: Costs vary widely depending on the treatment type, country, hospital, and length of care — CAR-T therapy and proton beam radiation are typically among the most expensive options, while standard chemotherapy protocols cost considerably less. Some countries offer significant cost savings compared to Western centres for equivalent care. Final costs should always be confirmed directly with the treating hospital based on your child's specific treatment plan.

items.q: Which countries offer advanced pediatric cancer treatment for international patients?
items.a: Specialized paediatric oncology programs, including CAR-T trials and proton beam therapy, are available at select centres in the United States, Europe, China, and other countries, though not every centre offers every treatment. Access depends on the specific diagnosis, the centre's paediatric expertise, and hospital acceptance. Confirming with individual treating centres is necessary before making travel plans.

items.q: What medical records are needed before seeking a second opinion for pediatric cancer?
items.a: Typically needed documents include the full pathology report, imaging studies (MRI, CT, or PET scans), any molecular or genomic testing already done, and a summary of treatment received so far. Complete, recent records allow a paediatric oncology specialist to give an accurate assessment. Missing test results can delay a thorough second opinion.

items.q: How do I find a specialist center for my child's specific cancer type?
items.a: Finding the right centre depends on matching your child's specific cancer subtype and treatment needs to hospitals with proven paediatric oncology expertise in that area, since not every centre treats every rare childhood cancer. Factors like CAR-T trial availability, proton therapy access, or sarcoma-specific programmes narrow the options. A specialist case review can help identify centres realistically suited to your child's diagnosis.

items.q: How does CancerFax help families access advanced pediatric cancer care?
items.a: CancerFax helps families review their child's pathology, imaging, and molecular testing, identify specialist paediatric oncology centres and relevant clinical trials globally, and coordinate travel, visa, and family support logistics. Treatment decisions are always made by the treating paediatric oncology team based on the child's full diagnosis and health status, not by CancerFax.
